q-120808:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,({tan}^{2}⁡\theta +1) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify and use $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sec}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta  \\  & =({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{tan}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

q-114060:
A function $f(x)$ is concave up over an interval $(a,b)$ if ${f}^{″}(x)>0$ for all $x\in (a,b).$

On the given graph of $y={f}^{″}(x),$ we can see that ${f}^{″}(x)>0$ on the intervals  $(-1,0)$ and  $(0,1).$  Therefore, the function $f(x)$ is concave up on the intervals  $(-1,0)$ and  $(0,1).$

q-60145:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-20{x}^{2}+60x-41) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x & =-41 \\ 20({x}^{2}-3x) & =-41 \\ 20[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}] & =-41 \\ 20[{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}] & =-41\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-20\cdot \frac{9}{4} & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-45 & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =45-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=4.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{4}{20} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{2}| & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

q-86414:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}+36x-94) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-12x] & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}] & =-94 \\ 3[{(x-6)}^{2}-36] & =-94\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-6)}^{2}-3\cdot 36 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2}-108 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =-94+108 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-6$, $q=14.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=14-(-6)=14+6=20.
$$

q-49332:
In this case, we have to use the identity  

$$
1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3}\frac{1-{cot}^{4}⁡x}{{cot}^{2}⁡x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3}\frac{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}{{cot}^{2}⁡x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3}(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x{|}_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\frac{2\pi }{3}-\operatorname{cot}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-18603:
The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)-{g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(2)={f}^{′}(2)-{g}^{′}(2).
$$

Also, notice that $x=2$ corresponds to 

- the interval $x\in (-2,3)$ for the function $f,$ and

- the interval $x\in (-2,3)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039683/assets/299b996bf08e4b4e8560d013829ddd1f42751767cd3f00dcd04c23c95f2c62b4.png)

- The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-2,3)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{1-1}{3-(-2)}=0.
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$

- The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in (-2,3)$ and equals

$$
\frac{Δg}{Δx}=\frac{3-(-2)}{3-(-2)}=1.
$$

Therefore, ${g}^{′}(2)=1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(2) & ={f}^{′}(2)-{g}^{′}(2) \\  & =0-1 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-105502:
The product rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)+f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(-3)={f}^{′}(-3)\cdot g(-3)+f(-3)\cdot {g}^{′}(-3).
$$

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-3)=-2$ and $g(-3)=0.$

Additionally,

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (-4,2)$ equals $1.$ So, ${f}^{′}(-3)=1.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (-4,-2)$ equals $3.$ So, ${g}^{′}(-3)=3.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(-3) & ={f}^{′}(-3)\cdot g(-3)+f(-3)\cdot {g}^{′}(-3) \\  & =1\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 3 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

q-113763:
First, we find the stationary points. Differentiating $f(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+6x+3 \\  & =3({x}^{2}+2x+1) \\  & =3(x+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ gives

$$
3(x+1)^{2}=0\,⇒\,x=-1.
$$

So $x=-1$ is the only stationary point of $f(x).$ Next, to determine whether this point is local maximum or minimum, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=-2,0$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-2) & =3(-2+1)^{2}=3>0 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3(0+1)^{2}=3>0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table shown below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $-2$ |  | $0$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ |  | $↗$ |

The first derivative does not change sign at $x=-1.$ Therefore, we conclude that $x=-1$ is neither a minimum nor a maximum.

Hence, the first derivative test shows that the function has no local extrema.

q-10832:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{{x}^{3}}-x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-12{x}^{-4}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=-12(1)^{-4}-1=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=-13$ and the coordinates of our point $(1,3),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(3) & =-13(x-1) \\ y & =-13x+13+3 \\ y & =-13x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

q-141116:
We're given that $y=\frac{1}{A+x}$ is the solution to the initial value problem. Therefore, it must satisfy the differential equation *and* the initial condition $y(0)=\frac{1}{2}.$

Substituting the initial condition $y(0)=\frac{1}{2}$ into our solution and solving for $A,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{A+x} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{A+0} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{A} \\ A & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\frac{1}{2+x}.
$$

q-73457:
First, we find the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}b\times c & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =((-1)\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot (-3))i-(2\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 3)j+(2\cdot (-3)-(-1)\cdot 3)k \\  & =-3i-3j-3k \\  & =⟨-3,-3,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =⟨1,-3,2⟩\cdot ⟨-3,-3,-3⟩ \\  & =1\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot (-3)+2\cdot (-3) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20054:
Remember that the scalar triple product $a\cdot (b\times c)$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $a,$ $b,$ and $c.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =(0\cdot 2-4\cdot 3)+(2\cdot 2-2\cdot 3)+2(2\cdot 4-2\cdot 0) \\  & =-12-2+16 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20059:
First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}3a\cdot (\sqrt{2}b\times 3c) & =18\sqrt{2} \\ 3\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot 3\cdot [a\cdot (b\times c)] & =18\sqrt{2} \\ a\cdot (b\times c) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $c$ and $b$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (c\times b) & =-2,\end{aligned}
$$

and again we swap $c$ and $a$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot (a\times b) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-18658:
First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}4a\cdot (-b\times c) & =12 \\ 4\cdot (-1)\cdot [a\cdot (b\times c)] & =12 \\ a\cdot (b\times c) & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $a$ and $b$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}b\cdot (a\times c) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-51054:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(-1)=(-1)^{2}+1=2,$ so $f(-1)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}({x}^{3}+x) \\  & =(-1)^{3}+(-1) \\  & =-2, \\ {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =(-1)^{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\,\,\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-1$ because ${lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x).$
